analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to correctly classify workers as employees or contractors and notify workers of their rights.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop worker misclassification never left the Senate committee, dying without a hearing, a vote, or a single Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every company that uses workers — including contractors — to classify them correctly as employees or non-employees and to give each new worker a written notice stating that classification, the worker's legal rights, and how to contact the Labor Department. Misclassifying an employee as a contractor would become a specific legal violation, with doubled damages and fines up to $5,000 per violation for repeat or willful offenders. It would also require states to audit for employers who dodge unemployment insurance and to penalize misclassification, and direct the Labor Department to share misclassification findings with the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are labeled "independent contractors" but are treated like employees — often denied minimum wage, overtime, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation — would gain a written notice of their status, a clear legal path to challenge it, and stronger penalties for employers who misclassify them. Honest businesses that follow the rules would compete on a more level playing field against firms that cut labor costs through misclassification. State unemployment funds and taxpayers would also recover payroll taxes and insurance contributions that misclassifying employers currently avoid.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every company using workers to classify them accurately and give each new worker a written notice of their classification, their legal rights, and the local Labor Department office — with a copy kept in the company's records.

Makes wrongly classifying an employee as a non-employee a specific violation of federal labor law, and protects any worker who complains about their classification from being fired or retaliated against.

Doubles the liquidated damages a worker can recover when an employer both violates wage or hour rules and misclassifies them, and sets civil penalties up to $1,100 per violation or up to $5,000 for repeat or willful violators.

Creates a presumption that a worker is an employee if the company never provided the required notice, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence — putting the burden of proving contractor status on the company, not the worker.

Requires states, as a condition of federal unemployment grants, to audit for employers that fail to register or pay unreported wages (which strips workers of unemployment coverage) and to impose penalties for misclassification and unreported pay.
Directs the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division to target audits at industries with frequent misclassification and to refer misclassification findings to the IRS for tax enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors would bear the cost: payroll taxes, unemployment insurance and workers' compensation contributions, overtime and minimum wage obligations for reclassified workers, new notice and recordkeeping requirements, and fines or doubled damages when they violate the rules. Some of those costs would likely be passed to customers or shared with contractors, and small businesses would face paperwork for the notice requirement even when their classifications are legitimate.

drawbacks.text: The notice and recordkeeping requirements apply to every company that engages any worker, including legitimate independent contractors, imposing new compliance paperwork on small businesses that have done nothing wrong.

The penalty structure — doubled liquidated damages plus per-worker civil fines and a strong presumption of employee status when notice is missing — raises litigation risk for businesses and could push some firms to stop using contractors altogether, reducing flexible arrangements some workers prefer.

Reclassified work would cost more, since employees must receive payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, and overtime that contractors do not; those costs would be passed to customers or absorbed in lower contractor earnings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: misclassification strips workers of wage, hour, and unemployment protections and shifts costs onto taxpayers and honest competitors. The costs are real too but narrower — paperwork for compliant businesses and higher prices where reclassification occurs. The bill's design leans heavily toward workers (the notice presumption and doubled damages), which makes enforcement strong but raises legitimate concerns about litigation exposure for businesses in gray areas. On balance it is a worker-protection bill whose costs fall mostly on firms currently benefiting from misclassification.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the bill on July 29, 2015, joined by five Democratic cosponsors including Elizabeth Warren, Sherrod Brown, and Patty Murray.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the only action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and no Republican senator cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that classify employees as independent contractors came out ahead: they continued to avoid payroll taxes, unemployment insurance contributions, and overtime obligations, with no federal penalty or notice requirement ever taking effect.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 6 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Franken, Murray, Warren, Brown, and Merkley.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor during the two years it sat in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All seven senators behind the bill were Democrats (the sponsor plus six Democratic cosponsors); no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-run committee took no action on it.

industries.note: These businesses are built on treating workers as independent contractors, avoiding payroll taxes, overtime, and unemployment insurance. The bill would make misclassification a specific federal violation with per-worker penalties and would target audits at industries with frequent misclassification.

industries.industry: Construction, trucking, and home-care firms using subcontractor models
industries.note: Industries where worker misclassification is common would face reclassification costs, doubled damages, and state unemployment audits under the bill. Its gain in avoided labor costs comes directly out of workers' protections and public insurance funds.

States would take on new auditing and penalty duties as a condition of federal grants, but would also recover contributions that misclassifying employers currently dodge, shoring up the unemployment trust funds that cover laid-off workers.
